title: Before you call it harmless—or condemn everyone who participates—there is a harder, more biblical question every follower of Jesus needs to face.
paragraphs: Before you call it harmless—or condemn everyone who participates—there is a harder, more biblical question every follower of Jesus needs to face.
There is a moment every October when the argument begins again.
One Christian posts, “Halloween is demonic. Christians should have nothing to do with it.”
Another replies, “Relax. My children are dressing like superheroes and collecting candy. We aren’t worshiping Satan.”
Someone posts a video about pagan origins.
Someone else points out that October 31 became associated with the eve of All Saints’ Day.

Parents become defensive. Churches divide into camps. One family attends a harvest festival. Another turns off the porch light. Another lets the children trick-or-treat but refuses frightening costumes. Another believes participating at all compromises their witness.
And somewhere underneath all the shouting is a sincere believer whispering a much quieter question:
“Jesus… what do You actually want from me?”
That is the question worth answering.
Not, “What will make other Christians approve of me?”
Not, “What does my culture consider normal?”
Not even merely, “Where did Halloween come from?”
But this:
Can I place what I am doing before Jesus Christ with a clean conscience and say, “Lord, this belongs to You”?
Because the most dangerous thing about Halloween may not be the costume hanging in your child’s bedroom.
It may be how easily Christians can spend hours arguing about darkness while ignoring the darkness hiding inside their own hearts.
Read that again.
A person can refuse Halloween and still secretly entertain pornography.
A person can throw away every plastic skeleton in the house and still harbor unforgiveness.
A person can condemn witches in October while practicing greed, gossip, lust, bitterness, pride, drunkenness, hatred, manipulation, envy, or hypocrisy the rest of the year.
And a person can also make the opposite mistake—using “Christian freedom” as an excuse to become comfortable with things Scripture explicitly tells believers to reject.
So this article is not going to give either side an easy escape.
Because Jesus did not die merely to make us culturally conservative.
And He did not die to make us culturally comfortable.
He died to make us His.
That changes the question completely.

Historically, what people today call “Halloween” is not reducible to one simple origin story. The name itself is connected with “All Hallows’ Eve,” the evening before All Saints’ Day, while customs associated with the modern holiday developed through a mixture of Christian observances, European folk traditions, and customs often connected by historians with Samhain and later cultural developments. That history is worth understanding, but history alone cannot settle the Christian’s moral responsibility.
Why?
Because Scripture does not contain the sentence, “Thou shalt not celebrate Halloween.”

But Scripture does give us principles strong enough to examine what we are doing, why we are doing it, what it communicates, what it awakens in us, how it affects others, and whether Christ can truly be glorified through it.
Paul dealt with a surprisingly relevant problem in Corinth.

Christians there lived in a culture saturated with pagan religion. One controversy involved food associated with idols. Paul did not respond with the simplistic principle that previous pagan association automatically made every subsequent ordinary use of an object sinful.

He could tell believers to eat food sold in the marketplace without conducting an investigation into its history for conscience’s sake (1 Corinthians 10:25–26). Yet in the very same chapter, he drew an uncompromising boundary against actual participation in idolatrous fellowship (1 Corinthians 10:20–21).
That distinction matters enormously.
Something having a complicated cultural history is not identical to a Christian personally participating in idolatry.
But neither does Christian liberty mean Christians may knowingly participate in occultism, divination, sorcery, spiritism, or the celebration of evil.
Scripture is unmistakably serious about those things.

Deuteronomy 18:10–12 condemns practices such as divination, sorcery, interpreting omens, witchcraft, mediums, spiritists, and attempts to consult the dead. Whatever debates Christians may have about costumes, candy, pumpkins, neighborhood gatherings, or October 31 itself, there should be no ambiguity here:
The follower of Jesus does not play with the occult.
We do not seek supernatural power apart from God.
We do not consult spirits.
We do not romanticize demonic powers.
We do not treat witchcraft as spiritually harmless merely because culture packages it as entertainment.
We belong to Jesus Christ.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5:11:
A careful sense of the Greek is:
“Do not participate with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather expose them.”

That word συγκοινωνεῖτε carries the idea of sharing in or participating together with something. Paul is not telling Christians to become terrified of the existence of darkness. He is telling them not to become participants in its works.
And that changes how we approach Halloween.
The biblical question cannot merely be, “Is October 31 pagan?”
The deeper questions are:
What exactly am I participating in?
What am I celebrating?
What am I teaching my children to admire?
What am I normalizing?
What is happening in my conscience?
What does my participation communicate to people around me?
And can I sincerely do this for the glory of God?
Paul gives us one of the most devastatingly simple tests in the New Testament:
“Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.” — 1 Corinthians 10:31
Notice the reach of that sentence.
Whatever you do.
That reaches the costume.
The decorations.
The movie.
The party.
The social-media post.
The joke.
The haunted attraction.
The church event.
The decision to participate.
The decision not to participate.
Even the way you speak about Christians whose conscience differs from yours.
Can you bring it underneath the lordship of Christ?
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Or perhaps you came wanting me to say, “Halloween is completely harmless,” so your conscience would stop bothering you.
Scripture refuses to serve either agenda so cheaply.
Romans 14 speaks directly to disagreements among believers over disputable matters.
Paul writes:
“One person regards one day above another; another regards every day alike…”
Then comes the principle:
“Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.” — Romans 14:5

The Greek verb κρίνει, krinei, can carry the sense of judging, evaluating, or regarding. Paul’s concern in Romans 14 is not that truth becomes subjective. Murder does not become righteous because somebody feels peaceful about it. Idolatry does not become acceptable because someone has “liberty.” Sexual immorality does not become holy because someone’s conscience has stopped protesting.
Romans 14 concerns matters in which believers can differ without overturning explicit commands of God.
That distinction protects us from two opposite errors.
Legalism says, “My personal conviction must become God’s command for everyone.”
License says, “My personal freedom allows me to ignore God’s commands.”
The Gospel gives us neither.
Jesus gives us freedom under His lordship.
So should Christians celebrate Halloween?
The most biblically responsible answer requires more maturity than a meme.

A Christian should never participate in actual occult practice, glorification of evil, divination, spiritism, witchcraft, satanic worship, or anything that requires fellowship with what Scripture calls darkness.
That boundary should not be blurry.

But whether every non-occult cultural activity associated with October 31—such as children receiving candy, wearing an innocent costume, visiting neighbors, sharing a meal, or attending a Christ-centered alternative event—is inherently sinful is much harder to establish from Scripture.
The Bible does not give us permission to manufacture commandments God did not give.
And it does not give us permission to ignore commandments He did give.
This means one Christian family may prayerfully decide, “We will not participate at all. Our conscience before Christ will not allow it.”
That family should not be mocked.
Another Christian family may say, “Our children will wear innocent costumes, visit neighbors, receive candy, and we will deliberately avoid occult imagery and anything celebrating evil.”
That family should not automatically be accused of worshiping demons merely because another believer has a stricter conviction.
But both families must answer to the same Lord.
And both need humility.
Romans 14:6 says that the person who observes a day should do so unto the Lord.
That phrase destroys superficial Christianity.
“Unto the Lord.”
Can you say that?
Not “because everyone does it.”
Not “because my children begged me.”
Not “because my church forbids it.”
Not “because Christians on Facebook told me what to think.”
Unto the Lord.
Jesus, this decision is Yours.
Jesus, these children are Yours.
Jesus, this home is Yours.
Jesus, my entertainment is Yours.
Jesus, my conscience is Yours.
Jesus, my freedom is Yours.
Jesus, even my October 31 is Yours.
And perhaps that is the confrontation some of us desperately need.
Because we have spent so much time asking how close Christians can stand to darkness without technically sinning that we have forgotten how breathtaking it is to walk in the Light.
The Christian life is not supposed to be a lifelong investigation into how much darkness we can safely tolerate.
We have something infinitely better.
Jesus said:
“I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.” — John 8:12
That is Christianity.
Not fear of darkness.
Not fascination with darkness.
Not legalistic obsession with darkness.
Christ.
The Light.
And maybe October 31 presents believers with an opportunity we have overlooked.
While houses around you are opening their doors…
open yours with love.
While neighbors who rarely speak to each other are walking the same streets…
learn their names.
While children knock at your door…
be kind.
While culture talks about death…
tell people about the One who conquered it.
Because Christianity possesses a message far more terrifying to hell than Christians hiding behind locked doors.
The tomb is empty.
Death lost.
Sin can be forgiven.
Satan has not won.
Jesus Christ was crucified, buried, and raised.
The King lives.
And the Gospel does not tell frightened sinners to clean themselves up enough to approach Him.
It announces that the holy Son of God entered our darkness to rescue us from it.
Think about that.
Jesus did not merely shout instructions into the darkness.
He came for people trapped inside it.
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.” — Luke 19:10
Maybe you are reading an article about Halloween, but something much more personal has started happening.
Because you know there is darkness in your life that has nothing to do with October.
Something nobody sees.
A secret relationship.
An addiction.
A browser history.
Bitterness toward someone who hurt you.
A habit you keep promising God you will quit.
A fascination with occult material that went farther than entertainment.
A private compromise.
A double life.
A wound you disguised as anger.
A prayer life that slowly disappeared.
A Bible gathering dust while your soul starves.
And suddenly the question is no longer:
“Should Christians celebrate Halloween?”
It is:
“What have I allowed into my heart?”
That question hurts.
But conviction is not the same thing as hopeless condemnation.
The Gospel does not expose your darkness so Jesus can stand at a distance and humiliate you.
The Gospel exposes darkness because Christ came to rescue sinners.
At the cross, Jesus carried sin.
Real sin.
Ugly sin.
Embarrassing sin.
The kind we confess publicly.
The kind we hope nobody ever discovers.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
Grace does not mean darkness was harmless.
Grace means darkness does not have to have the final word.
Repentance is not God demanding that you save yourself.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who can.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Come home.
Maybe you compromised.
Come home.
Maybe you knew better.
Come home.
Maybe your conscience has been whispering for months and you kept drowning it out.
Come home.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
That is why our message will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites the story of the addict.
The hypocrite.
The prodigal.
The religious person secretly dying inside.
The skeptic who thought Christianity had nothing left to say.
The believer who wandered farther than anyone knows.
He does not rewrite evil by pretending it was good.
He rewrites sinners by forgiving, cleansing, redeeming, and transforming those who come to Him in repentance and faith.
So before deciding what your family will do this Halloween, do something more important than searching for another argument online.
Pray.
Open Scripture.
Ask whether the activity itself violates God’s Word.
Ask what it celebrates.
Ask what it communicates.
Ask whether it could wound another believer’s conscience.
Ask what it is teaching your children.
Ask whether your own conscience is clear.
And finally ask:
“Jesus, can I genuinely do this for Your glory?”
If the answer is no, walk away.
You do not need what you cannot offer to Christ.
If your conscience remains troubled, do not violate it merely because other Christians tell you to relax. Romans 14:23 gives a sobering principle: whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.
And if your conscience permits something Scripture does not prohibit, do not turn your freedom into arrogance.
Love is more important than proving how free you are.
Likewise, if you abstain, do not turn abstinence into spiritual pride.
Holiness is not measured by how many people you can condemn.
It is possible to avoid Halloween and still miss Jesus.
It is possible to win the argument and lose tenderness.
It is possible to expose darkness everywhere except the place God wanted to expose first:
inside us.
So whether your porch light is on or off this October, make certain another Light is burning.
Christ in you.
Let your children remember that Jesus was more beautiful to you than fear.
Let your neighbors discover that Christians are not merely people famous for what they oppose, but people transformed by the Savior they adore.
Let darkness remind you of the Light.
Let death remind you of resurrection.
Let costumes remind you how exhausting it is to spend your life pretending to be someone you are not.
Take off the spiritual mask.
Jesus already knows.
And He is still calling.

And if you disagree with parts of this article, you are welcome here too. Open your Bible. Test what was written. Speak with grace. We do not need another Christian shouting match. We need believers learning to search Scripture, love one another, repent quickly, and submit everything to Jesus.
Supporting Gospel ministry should never be presented as a requirement for earning God’s favor or proving that you glorify Him—salvation and grace cannot be purchased.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the struggling Christian.
Invite the person who walked away from church.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the lukewarm believer.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Jesus could never want someone with their history.
Because perhaps the greatest answer Christians can give to a culture fascinated with darkness is not panic.
It is a life so surrendered to Jesus that the darkness cannot explain the light coming from it.
And when October 31 finally arrives, remember this:
The question is not merely whether you walked past the darkness—the question is whether the world could see Christ’s Light walking through you.
